questions.q: Why does finding implied volatility require a numerical solver like Newton-Raphson instead of just rearranging the Black-Scholes formula algebraically?
options: Volatility appears inside a cumulative normal distribution in the Black-Scholes formula, which isn't algebraically invertible in closed form
Black-Scholes was never designed to be solved for volatility under any circumstances
Newton-Raphson is simply a stylistic preference with no mathematical necessity
Implied volatility can always be read directly off the option's price with no calculation needed
questions.explain: The cumulative normal distribution in the formula has no closed-form inverse, which is exactly why a numerical root-finding method is required instead of algebraic rearrangement.

questions.q: What role does vega play in the Newton-Raphson implied volatility solver?
options: Vega is the slope of the Black-Scholes price with respect to volatility, used to determine how much to adjust the volatility guess at each iteration
Vega is only used to validate the final answer, not during the iteration process
Vega has no functional role in this solver and is only shown for reference
Vega replaces the need for an initial volatility guess entirely
questions.explain: Each Newton-Raphson step divides the price error by vega to determine the next volatility guess -- vega IS the slope the method uses to converge.

questions.q: In the worked example, why is implied volatility highest at the lowest strike (80) and lowest near-the-money (100), rather than flat across all strikes?
options: The market is pricing in a higher probability of a sharp downside move than a constant-volatility model predicts -- real crash-protection demand bids up low-strike option prices and their implied volatility
This pattern indicates a calculation error in the implied volatility solver
Implied volatility is always identical across every strike in real markets
The pattern is random and has no real market interpretation
questions.explain: A flat smile would mean Black-Scholes's constant-volatility assumption holds exactly -- the real skew reflects genuine market pricing of downside risk, not noise or error.

questions.q: What is the difference between a volatility smile and a volatility surface?
options: A smile is implied volatility plotted against strike for one fixed expiry; a surface adds the second dimension by repeating the fit across every available expiry
They are two different names for exactly the same thing
A smile only applies to call options; a surface only applies to put options
A surface is computed without using Newton-Raphson, unlike a smile
questions.explain: The surface is the smile's strike dimension combined with a second, expiry dimension -- fitting implied volatility at every strike AND every available expiry.

questions.q: Why does Newton-Raphson converge quickly (typically under 10 iterations) for this specific implied-volatility problem?
options: Vega is a smooth, well-behaved, almost-always-positive function for realistic option parameters, which is exactly the condition Newton-Raphson needs to converge reliably
Newton-Raphson always converges in exactly one iteration regardless of the function
The solver uses a fixed, pre-computed lookup table instead of actual iteration
Fast convergence only happens when the strike exactly equals the current stock price
questions.explain: Newton-Raphson's reliability depends on the slope function (vega here) being smooth and consistently signed -- exactly the property that makes this particular root-finding problem well-behaved.
